subject: Business Models
title: Singer Sewing Machines: The First Franchise
description: One-minute skill: Singer Sewing Machines: The First Franchise.

hook.text: In 1851, Isaac Singer had a great sewing machine but no way to sell it nationwide. He invented franchising.

buildup.text: Singer licensed salespeople to demo and sell machines in exclusive territories. Each bought inventory at wholesale.

discovery.text: This let Singer scale nationally without building stores. Licensees invested their own money and effort.

twist.text: Singer also pioneered installment payments: buy the machine now, pay monthly. Leasing and franchising together.

climax.text: Singer became the world's first multinational corporation. Franchising enabled global scale in the 1800s.

punchline.text: Sewing machines in 1851 invented franchising. The model is 170 years old.

quiz.question: Who is credited with creating the first franchise model?

details.summary: Isaac Singer created the first franchise system in the 1850s by licensing independent operators to sell and service Singer sewing machines in designated territories..
details.whyItMatters: Singer's franchise model invented the core mechanics still used today: territorial licenses, training requirements, brand standards, and the balance between franchisor control and franchisee independence..
takeaways: Singer created the franchise model in the 1850s to distribute sewing machines
Licensed operators received exclusive territories with training and brand standards
The model solved distribution challenges before national retail chains existed

faq.question: Why did Singer need to invent franchising?
faq.answer: Sewing machines were expensive, mechanically complex products that required demonstration and after-sale service. Singer could not afford to open company-owned stores nationwide..

faq.question: How was Singer's franchise model similar to modern franchising?
faq.answer: Singer granted exclusive territories, provided training, set brand and service standards, required minimum sales volumes, and retained the right to terminate underperforming operators. These elements form the backbone of every modern franchise agreement 170 years later.
